competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every item shows three tiled cases and asks 'Which rule always gives the number of tiles?' or its variant, and the keyed rules 'length × width' and 'side × side' are the two formulas the competency names; across all fourteen samples only the keyed rule survives all three cases, so no offered option is a second valid answer. Three rectangle items nevertheless hold one dimension fixed in every case: seed 43 runs 'a 7 by 10 rectangle takes 70 tiles' then 8 by 10 then 9 by 10, seed 46 fixes the 4 and seed 604 fixes the 5. Those case sets never vary the width, so they cannot demonstrate that the count depends on it, and the counts form an arithmetic run that a narrower add-a-constant pattern fits equally well. On those three the derivation is only half shown.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both shapes the competency names are present: six square items keyed 'side × side' and eight rectangle items keyed 'length × width', so both formulas get derived rather than only one. Each stem states the tiling explicitly, for example 'Cover each square with unit square tiles and count them', and one rectangle item pairs 'a 2 by 5 rectangle takes 10 tiles' with 'a 5 by 2 rectangle takes 10 tiles' so the commutative reading of the tile array is exposed too. Nothing in the set asks for anything outside the derivation itself.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The grade 3 quarter 1 load is reasonable: the learner reads three worked tile counts and picks one of four rules stated in ordinary words, with no letter variables, no exponent notation and no unit labels. The heaviest step is checking that 'side × side' reproduces the counts in 'a 2 by 2 square takes 4 tiles' and its two partners, which is pattern matching over basic facts rather than symbolic manipulation, and the tiling sentence keeps the concrete referent in front of the learner.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Thirteen of the fourteen rendered stems are distinct, edge lengths range from 2 to 10, and the case triples differ from item to item. Two sentence frames are in play: 'Cover each rectangle with unit square tiles and count them' and 'Three squares are tiled with unit squares', the latter closing with 'Which rule works for every one of them?' instead of the standard closing question. The correct option also moves among the four key positions. One blemish only: seeds 50 and 502 render the same item character for character, differing solely in the declared formatter.

competency_alignment.rationale: The samples sit on the exact wording of the competency, which is inductive derivation using square tile units. Tiles are the stated medium in every stem, for example 'Three rectangles are tiled with unit squares'; what is requested is a rule and not a numeric area; and the keyed rules 'length × width' and 'side × side' are precisely the two formulas named. Nothing reaches past the clause into square unit notation, unit conversion, or computing an area for a figure that was never tiled.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Edge lengths run from 2 to 10 and tile counts from 4 up to 100, the largest case being 'a 10 by 10 square takes 100 tiles'; every product lies inside the basic multiplication table a grade 3 learner works with, and small cases such as 'a 4 by 3 rectangle takes 12 tiles' keep at least one genuinely countable array in view in most items.
